n: Eliphaz, probably the oldest of the friends, speaks first. This begins three rounds of speeches between Job and his friends (chapters 4–27). Keep in mind that at the end God says the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).
He begins politely: Will you be upset if we speak? But I can’t keep quiet.
Eliphaz reminds Job that he once taught and strengthened many weak people.
Job’s words used to lift up the stumbling and steady trembling knees. This image is echoed later in scripture as a call to serve.
Now that trouble has hit Job himself, Eliphaz says, he falls apart. It’s a gentle jab: you could give advice, but can you take it?
Shouldn’t your reverence for God and your upright life give you confidence and hope? Eliphaz assumes a righteous person has nothing to fear.

Here is Eliphaz’s core belief: innocent people never perish; only the wicked are destroyed. The book of Job challenges this simple formula — and so does the life of Jesus, the innocent One who suffered.

f.g: The friends’ view: suffering always proves sin. The book as a whole rejects this.

n: From his experience, those who plant evil harvest evil. That is a true principle in general — but Eliphaz wrongly applies it to every case of suffering.
The wicked are destroyed by a blast of God’s breath, like plants withered by a hot wind.
Eliphaz compares the wicked to fierce lions whose roar is silenced and teeth are broken. Five different Hebrew words for “lion” are used in verses 10–11.

f.g: Hebrew has many words for lions; this poem uses five of them.

n: Even strong lions die without prey, and their cubs scatter. The wicked, however powerful, eventually fall.
Eliphaz claims a secret revelation — a message whispered to him.
It came in disturbing night visions, during deep sleep.

f.g: The same word used of Adam’s and Abram’s deep sleep (Genesis 2:21; 15:12).

n: He was seized by fear and trembling until his bones shook.

f.w: made all my bones to shake

n: A spirit or breath of wind passed by his face, and his hair stood on end. The scene is eerie and mysterious.

f.g: Hebrew ruach — can mean spirit, wind, or breath.

n: A shadowy form stood before him in silence, and then he heard a voice. It is an unsettling vision — and we may wonder whether its source was truly divine.

f.w: there was silence, and I heard a voice

n: The message: Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or purer than his Maker? It is true in itself, but Eliphaz uses it to imply Job must be guilty.

f.w: Shall mortal man be more just than God?

n: Even God’s heavenly servants and angels can’t be fully trusted by Him, the vision says, and He charges them with error.

f.g: Found fault with, accused of error.

n: How much less can He trust humans, living in fragile bodies of clay, who can be crushed as easily as a moth.

f.g: Mortal bodies made from the dust (Genesis 2:7; 2 Corinthians 5:1).
Crushed as easily as a moth.

n: Human life is fragile: between morning and evening people die, and they vanish without anyone noticing.
Their life is pulled up like a tent cord, and they die without ever gaining wisdom. Eliphaz’s point: humble yourself, Job, for you are mortal and flawed.

f.w: their excellency which is in them go away
f.g: Many translate it “their tent cord is pulled up” — an image of death.
